periods.activity_title: Reading the Memorial Poem Aloud Together

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.161): read aloud and recite the poem with the class.

time_bands.activity: Open the textbook to the poem and ask students what they know about war memorials. Take two or three brief responses to warm up attention and set a respectful tone.

Read the poem aloud slowly and clearly, line by line, while students follow in their books. Pause after each couplet to let the images — the eternal flame, names etched in stone, battlefields and oceans — register.
Lead a whole-class recitation of the poem, first with teacher support and then without. Encourage students to match the solemn, steady tone the couplet structure calls for.
Invite volunteers to recite a couplet of their choice and say in one sentence what image it creates. Close by asking students to read the poem silently once more and begin committing it to memory.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem is a recitation piece built entirely on couplets — behold/retold, pride/confide, wide/side — so the end-rhyme is the scaffolding for memorisation; point this out explicitly. A common difficulty is that students rush the lines and lose the solemn register; model a measured pace and ask them to mirror it. Students who find public recitation daunting should be invited to recite in pairs or small groups rather than alone.
materials: Textbook open to the poem, p.160–161

periods.activity_title: Exploring the Memorial — Research and Reflection

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.161): find three facts about the memorial and share with class.

time_bands.activity: Briefly recall the poem's central images — the eternal flame, names etched in stone, soldiers from battlefields, skies, and oceans. Ask: what would you want to find out about the actual memorial that the poem hints at but does not tell you?

Students work in pairs or small groups to note down three facts about the National War Memorial using any available resource in the classroom — textbook, reference books, or the teacher's prepared fact-sheet. Each group records their facts clearly in their notebooks.

Groups share one fact each in a quick round; teacher notes distinct facts on the board to avoid repetition and adds context — when the memorial was established, where it stands, and what the four concentric circles represent.

Each student writes three to four sentences in their notebook: two facts they found most striking and one reason they would want to visit the memorial. Students who finish quickly may sketch a simple diagram labelling the eternal flame and the stone walls.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read and recited the poem's tribute to the memorial, students are now ready to anchor its imagery in factual knowledge — the poem mentions the eternal flame and names etched in stone, both of which correspond to real features of the memorial. A common difficulty is that students conflate the National War Memorial with other monuments; clarify that it was inaugurated in February 2019 and is distinct from India Gate. Students without internet access at home should complete their fact-finding entirely in this sitting using the teacher's fact-sheet.
materials: Teacher-prepared fact-sheet about the National War Memorial (printed or written on the board)

periods.activity_title: Poem, Memorial and Memory — A Whole-Chapter Synthesis

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.161): recite the full poem from memory and analyse its key devices.
Let us explore (p.161): connect poem imagery to real memorial features; discuss a planned visit.

time_bands.activity: Invite students to recite the poem from memory — in unison first, then one couplet each around the room. Celebrate the collective performance and ask: which line stayed with you most, and why?

Guide students through a close reading of three literary devices the poem uses: the anaphora in 'Each name etched, each stone, each story'; the personification of the eternal flame glowing 'in silence'; and the apostrophe 'let's always remember'. For each device, ask students to say what effect it has on the reader's feeling toward the soldiers.

Draw two columns on the board — 'What the poem says' and 'What the memorial actually has'. Students call out connections: the eternal flame (poem image ↔ real Amar Jawan Jyoti-style flame), names etched in stone (poem ↔ inscribed tablets), battlefields/skies/oceans (poem ↔ the three services the memorial honours). Discuss how the poet chose imagery that maps onto a real place.

Students write a short paragraph — five to six sentences — titled 'Why the National War Memorial Matters to Me', drawing on both the poem's language and the facts studied. Students share one sentence aloud to close the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together the poem's literary craft and the factual knowledge of the memorial — students can now see how the poet translated a real, physical place into solemn verse. Where students quote the poem in their paragraph, encourage them to use the exact words rather than paraphrasing, so the poem's formal register carries into their writing. Any student who finds the literary-device analysis unfamiliar should be invited to describe the effect of a line in their own words first; the technical term can follow the description.
materials: Board and chalk or marker for two-column comparison

items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 160 beginning "The eternal flame, in silence it glows". Which word rhymes with "glows" in the following couplet, and what does that rhyming pair suggest about the soldiers being honoured?

options.label: A
options.text: "blows" — the flame blows in the wind as a sign of restlessness.

options.label: B
options.text: "flows" — the flame flows like a river in memory of the fallen.

options.label: C
options.text: "rows" — the soldiers stood in neat rows during ceremonies.

options.label: D
options.text: "shows" — together the pair suggests that the flame quietly reveals the soldiers' courage to all who visit.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Students who choose this impose a visual ceremonial image not present in the poem and miss the couplet's pairing.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Suggests the student is choosing a rhyme by sound alone without checking that 'flows' appears in the couplet.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Introduces movement that contradicts the poem's tone of stillness and silence around the flame.

items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 160 beginning "Each name etched, each stone, each story". The poet repeats the word 'each' three times in this line. What effect does this repetition create, and how does it fit the solemn tone of the poem as a whole? Write your answer in two to three sentences.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The repetition of 'each' (anaphora) slows the line down and forces the reader to pause on every individual name, stone, and story, suggesting that no soldier's sacrifice is minor or forgotten. This steady, deliberate rhythm matches the poem's solemn, reverent tone throughout, where phrases like 'in silence it glows' and 'forever remind' also resist hurry.

items.item_stem: The poem refers to soldiers from 'battle fields', 'skies', and 'oceans wide'. The National War Memorial was built to honour the armed forces of Bharat. Write three facts about the National War Memorial — one about when or where it was established, one about the eternal flame or the inscribed names, and one about which armed services it honours.

expected_elements: States the memorial was inaugurated in February 2019 in New Delhi.
Mentions the eternal flame or names engraved on stone tablets.
Names all three services: Army, Navy, and Air Force.
Uses clear, factual sentences without copying the poem's language.

items.item_stem: The poem says 'The eternal flame, in silence it glows, / Paying homage to their courage that shows.' Imagine you are planning a visit to the National War Memorial. Write a short note of five to six sentences explaining what you would observe at the memorial, why the eternal flame matters, and what you would feel standing before the inscribed names of the soldiers.

expected_elements: Names at least one specific feature: flame, inscribed names, or stone walls.
Explains the significance of the eternal flame in own words.
Expresses a personal feeling or reflection about the soldiers' sacrifice.
Uses respectful, thoughtful language appropriate to the memorial context.
